summary: Defines a base solution for Diameter overload control, called Diameter Overload Indication Conveyance. It lets a Diameter node tell others that it is overloaded.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC lets a busy Diameter server ask nearby servers to send it fewer requests. The request travels inside the ordinary Diameter messages the servers already exchange, so no new protocol and no new traffic are needed.

subtitle: How Diameter nodes ask each other to send less traffic while one of them is overloaded.

tldr.problem: A Diameter node that is overloaded needs a way to ask other nodes to stop sending it so much work, and every Diameter application needs that ability without changing the base protocol.
tldr.mechanism: Nodes add new attribute-value pairs to messages they already exchange. One pair announces support and picks an abatement algorithm, another carries the overload report, and reacting nodes then cut the requested share of traffic by diverting or throttling requests.
tldr.outcome: Overload control works between any Diameter nodes that implement it, and nodes that do not can still be served by an agent that does. The RFC is a base solution and has been updated by RFC 8581.

today: RFC 7683 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2015. It has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 8581. The RFC calls itself a base solution and leaves agent overload, further traffic abatement algorithms and a dedicated error diagnostic to later specifications.

sections.title: Why Diameter Needs Overload Control
sections.content:
Diameter is the protocol used for authentication, authorization and accounting. A Diameter node that cannot keep up with the requests it receives becomes overloaded, and the work it wastes hurts the other nodes as well. This RFC defines a base solution for Diameter overload control, called Diameter Overload Indication Conveyance (DOIC), built on the requirements in RFC 7068.

DOIC needs no change to the Diameter base protocol in RFC 6733. A new Diameter application can make the mechanism mandatory by referencing this document, and the designers of that application then decide how overload control works for it. The solution is designed for existing and future applications, and it can be deployed in networks where some Diameter nodes do not implement it at all.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC lets a busy Diameter server ask other servers to send it fewer requests. It adds that ability without changing the Diameter protocol itself.

sections.title: Reporting Nodes and Reacting Nodes
sections.content:
Any Diameter node can take part in DOIC: clients, servers and agents alike. A node that sends an overload report is a reporting node, and a node that acts on such a report is a reacting node. The role follows the message type rather than the device, because the sender of a request acts as the reacting node and the sender of the answer acts as the reporting node. One node can hold both roles at once, and a reporting node may report overload on behalf of other nodes.

No new Diameter application and no new messages are defined. Nodes piggyback the DOIC information on messages they already exchange, by adding the AVPs OC-Supported-Features and OC-OLR to ordinary requests and answers. A report applies to the realm and the application of the message that carries it, so a node can support DOIC for one application and not for another, and can use different parameters for each.

Two report types are defined. A HOST_REPORT says that one host is overloaded, so reacting nodes divert or throttle the requests they route to that host. A REALM_REPORT says that a whole realm is overloaded, so reacting nodes treat the requests they route to that realm instead. Report types are extensible, and a later specification can define more.
sections.plainLanguage: The node that reports overload and the node that reacts to the report can be the same device. The information rides inside ordinary Diameter messages, so nothing new has to be set up on the network.

sections.title: Capability Announcement
sections.content:
Before a node reports overload, it needs to know that someone on the other side will act on the report. The DOIC Capability Announcement mechanism (DCA) does this with the OC-Supported-Features AVP, which is separate from the Diameter Capability Exchange. The first DOIC node on the path of a request adds the AVP to that request, and the reporting node returns the AVP in its answer. The presence of the AVP in the request is what tells the reporting node that a reacting node exists for that transaction.

Inside the AVP, the OC-Feature-Vector AVP carries a 64-bit field of feature bits. The bit OLR_DEFAULT_ALGO (0x0000000000000001) says that the loss algorithm is supported, and every DOIC node must always advertise it. The reporting node selects exactly one abatement algorithm and names it in its own feature vector, and the reacting node must use that algorithm if traffic reduction is requested.

A Diameter agent that supports DOIC can act on behalf of endpoints that do not. It adds the AVP to requests that lack it, and it may modify the AVP to reflect the mixture of features on each side. The RFC leaves the rules for deciding what to change to implementation decisions, but the agent must behave as a fully compliant reporting node downstream and as a fully compliant reacting node upstream.
sections.plainLanguage: Before sending an overload report, a node adds a feature field to its request. The reply says which traffic-cutting algorithm the other end will use. An agent can stand in for a device that does not support the mechanism.

sections.title: The Overload Control AVPs
sections.content:
Seven AVPs carry the DOIC information. OC-Supported-Features (code 621, Grouped) announces support and holds the feature vector. OC-Feature-Vector (622, Unsigned64) is the 64-bit flag field, and the value zero is reserved. OC-OLR (623, Grouped) is the report itself; it contains OC-Sequence-Number (624, Unsigned64), OC-Report-Type (626, Enumerated) and, optionally, OC-Reduction-Percentage (627, Unsigned32) and OC-Validity-Duration (625, Unsigned32). None of these AVPs may set the M-bit.

The OC-Validity-Duration AVP states in seconds how long a report stays valid, measured from the arrival of the first report with that sequence number. Its default value is 30 seconds and its maximum value is 86,400 seconds (24 hours). A value above the maximum is ignored and the default applies instead.

The OC-Reduction-Percentage AVP states the share of traffic the sender wants reduced, compared with what it would otherwise send. The value is between zero and one hundred, and a larger value is ignored. A value of 100 means that all traffic is to be throttled, because the reporting node is under severe load, and a value of 0 means that the node is stable and needs no abatement at all.
sections.plainLanguage: The information travels in seven new fields. Two matter most: how long the report stays valid, and what share of traffic should be cut. A report lasts 30 seconds by default and at most 24 hours.

sections.title: Overload Reports and Overload Control State
sections.content:
Both kinds of node keep an Overload Control State (OCS) for every active overload. A reacting node keeps one host-type entry for each destination host to which it sends host-routed requests, and one realm-type entry for each destination realm to which it sends realm-routed requests. Each entry holds the sequence number, the time of expiry, the selected algorithm and the data that algorithm needs, such as the reduction percentage.

When an answer arrives carrying an OC-OLR AVP, the reacting node decides whether the report belongs to a known overload condition. If it does, a sequence number greater than the stored one updates the entry, and a sequence number less than or equal to the stored one is ignored, so a repeated or stale report changes nothing. A wrap of the counter, recognized as a jump from within 1% of the maximum value to within 1% of the minimum, also updates the entry. A report whose validity duration is zero marks the condition as ended, and the RFC advises keeping the entry for a while so that traffic can return gradually instead of all at once.

A reporting node keeps an entry for each application, report type and algorithm, holding the sequence number, the validity duration, the expiration time and the algorithm data. The sequence number of a new condition starts at zero and must be greater than any number still in use for the same application and report type, and that rule has to hold across a restart of the node. The number is increased every time the contents of an entry change, and an entry with a validity duration of zero is kept long enough for the reacting nodes to delete theirs.
sections.plainLanguage: Each node keeps a small record of every active overload. A newer report replaces an older one, and a repeated or stale report is ignored, so a node always works from the most recent instruction.

sections.title: The Loss Algorithm
sections.content:
The loss algorithm is the one algorithm that every DOIC node must support, and it is stateless. A reporting node asks for a percentage reduction in the number of requests it would otherwise send, and the reacting node applies the treatment to that share of the requests it generates. The RFC sets out the steps at the reacting node: store or update the report, generate a request, check whether an active report covers that request, and then decide. One approach is to pick a random number between 1 and 100 and to treat the request when that number is less than or equal to the requested percentage; the other requests get normal routing.

Because the algorithm keeps no history, it cannot promise an absolute drop in traffic. It promises that the requested share of new requests gets the treatment.

Two treatments are defined. Diversion sends the request to another destination or along another path, and it is the preferred treatment when the overloaded node is not part of that path. Throttling limits the number of requests sent, either by a client deciding not to send, or by an agent or server rejecting the request with an error. Throttling is required when diversion is not possible or was not applied, and the result is a permanent rejection of that transaction.

When a report expires, the RFC advises the reacting node to return to full traffic in a controlled way, for example by sending probe messages first after a period of 100% reduction, so that the overloaded node does not slip back into overload.
sections.plainLanguage: The loss algorithm asks for a share of requests to be cut, and the node picks that share at random. It prefers to send the request somewhere else, and rejects it only when there is nowhere else to send it.

sections.title: Rejecting Requests Under Overload
sections.content: When a DOIC node rejects a request because it is overloaded, it chooses an error code from the chance that the request could succeed on another path. If the same request might succeed elsewhere, the node sends DIAMETER_TOO_BUSY. If the request would come back to the same node, for example because it carried a Destination-Host AVP naming that node, the node sends DIAMETER_UNABLE_TO_COMPLY, because retrying would only consume valuable resources during the overload. An agent that throttles on behalf of a client that does not support DOIC will generally use DIAMETER_UNABLE_TO_COMPLY.
sections.plainLanguage: A rejected request gets one of two error codes. The node says the network is too busy when trying another path could work, and says it cannot comply when the request would come back to the same node.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Overload reports are a denial-of-service risk. A series of injected realm reports asking for a 100% reduction could stop all traffic to that realm, and Diameter is often used to control access, so the effect can spread to the traffic of a whole network. Diameter nodes must not honor or forward reports from peers that are not trusted to send them, and they must strip the DOIC AVPs from messages that arrive from such peers. Reports can also reveal the state of a network, so a node must not send a report to a peer that is not authorized to receive it, and an agent must remove reports that other nodes inserted before forwarding a message to such a peer.

Two weaknesses are inherited from Diameter itself, which has no end-to-end authentication, integrity protection or confidentiality. Any agent on the path can read or change a report, so trust in a report from a distant node rests on trust in a chain of neighbors. The RFC also asks implementations to check that an answer carrying a report is a well-formed response to a request that is still pending, and that it arrived over a protected transport connection. Operators must be able to choose which peers may deliver reports and which may forward them.
sections.plainLanguage: Overload reports can be abused to shut traffic down, so a node only acts on reports from peers it trusts. Diameter has no end-to-end protection, which means every agent on the path can read or change a report.

items.desc: Unsigned64; increasing counter for the reports of one overload.

items.desc: Unsigned32; share of traffic to cut, from 0 to 100.
